title: Employment rights essentials
summary: What a contract of employment is, where its terms come from, and what to do when the written details and the contract do not match.

sections.title: What a contract of employment is
sections.body:
Every employee has an employment contract with their employer. It sets out the working conditions, rights, responsibilities and duties that apply to the job.
A contract begins when a person accepts a job offer. It does not have to be in writing to be valid.
Both sides must keep to the contract until it ends, or until its terms change. A change usually needs both sides to agree.
key_points: A contract starts when a job offer is accepted
A contract does not have to be written down
Changing its terms usually needs both sides to agree

sections.title: Where the terms come from
sections.body:
Terms can be written or spoken. They can be in a staff handbook or an offer letter, set by law, or come from a collective agreement.
Some terms apply even when nobody has written them down. A safe workplace is one example. Long-standing practice that both sides rely on can also become a term.
key_points: Terms can be written or spoken
Handbooks and offer letters can contain terms
Some unwritten terms still apply, such as a safe workplace

sections.title: Collective agreements
sections.body:
Some terms are agreed between an employer and a trade union or a staff association. This is a collective agreement.
It can cover pay, working hours, and which staff it applies to. If you are covered by one, it forms part of your terms.
key_points: A collective agreement is negotiated with a union or staff association
It can cover pay, hours and who is included

sections.title: The written statement of employment particulars
sections.body:
An employer must give each employee a written statement of employment particulars. This statement sets out the key terms, such as pay and hours.
The statement is not the contract itself. It is a document that records the main terms, and a fuller statement can follow. Changes to the terms must also be notified in writing, within the time limits the guidance sets out.
key_points: The written statement records the main terms
It is not the contract itself
Changes must be notified in writing

sections.title: When the written details seem wrong
sections.body:
Sometimes the written statement does not match what was agreed. The usual first step is to try to put it right informally, with the employer.
If that does not work, the next step is a grievance. Going to an employment tribunal is the last resort, after the earlier steps have been tried.
key_points: An employment tribunal is the last resort

sections.title: Where to get help
sections.body:
Acas gives advice on employment rights, contracts and disputes. It is a good first stop before you decide on any formal step.
The rules on contracts and terms are set out in GOV.UK guidance. Read the source page for the detail, because this course summarises it.
key_points: The GOV.UK guidance has the detail

questions.prompt: When does an employment contract start?
options: When the employee signs the contract
When a job offer is accepted
On the first day of work
When the first wages are paid
questions.explanation: A contract begins once a job offer is accepted. Signing a document or starting work does not change when it began.

questions.prompt: Must an employment contract be in writing?
options: No, it does not have to be written down
questions.explanation: A contract does not have to be written to exist. Its terms can be written or spoken.

questions.prompt: Which of these can be a source of contract terms?
options: A staff handbook or an offer letter
questions.explanation: Terms can come from handbooks, offer letters, the law and collective agreements, as well as from the contract itself.

questions.prompt: What is the written statement of employment particulars?
options: The whole contract, word for word
A written document that sets out the key terms, and is not itself the contract
A form the employee signs only at the end of the job
questions.explanation: The written statement records the main terms, such as pay and hours. It is not the contract itself.

questions.prompt: If the written details seem wrong, what is the usual first step?
options: Go straight to an employment tribunal
Try to put it right informally with the employer
questions.explanation: The usual first step is an informal conversation. A grievance comes next, and a tribunal is the last resort.
